extracted.intended_audience: news consumers, media critics, and journalists/editors
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and lessons for assessing the reliability of news reporting and for newsroom practices that prevent fabrication. Focuses on editorial verification, documentation, and reader skepticism informed by the Janet Cooke/'Jimmy's World' case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors must insist on knowing and verifying
rubrics_metrics.description: “Editors have to insist on knowing and verifying. That’s one of the big reasons they hold their jobs.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page argues editors should not simply trust reporters; they must actively verify key facts and not delegate full responsibility to reporters. Failure to do so is described as a systemic newsroom failure (example: Post editors standing by Cooke and later admitting they waived checks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Support conclusions with factual details that can be verified elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: “An honest news story will support its conclusions with factual details that can be verified elsewhere.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories should include identifiable, checkable facts and corroboration so independent parties can confirm claims. The absence of verifiable details is singled out as a hallmark of dishonest or fake reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert for quotes or facts that won’t withstand scrutiny (fake-news indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Fake news will include quotes or facts that won’t withstand scrutiny.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use attempted fact-checking of quotes and factual claims as a test: if key quotes or facts cannot be corroborated, treat the story with suspicion. The article cites the Cooke story’s uncorroborated quotes and invented interviewees as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not waive editorial rules about names, places, and other safeguards
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should not waive rules (e.g., about names and places) simply to get a compelling story into print.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece criticizes the Post for waiving such rules and overlooking warning signs because the story was compelling. Adherence to standard safeguards is recommended to catch fabrications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require and examine reporters' original notes and recordings
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should demand and review reporters' notes, tapes, and other primary reporting materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Post investigation found no notes of Cooke’s first supposed encounters with Jimmy and contradictory tape-recorded interviews — lack of documentation was a red flag. The rubric implies routine checking of source materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify reporters' credentials and autobiographical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify staffers' claimed qualifications and background (e.g., academic credentials) rather than accepting them at face value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Pulitzer committee discovered Cooke's false academic claims, which contributed to uncovering the fraud. Verifying credentials is presented as part of due diligence on reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat anonymous sources with special skepticism and extra verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Promises of total anonymity require additional vetting because anonymity can be used to conceal falsification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes an editor urged offering "total anonymity," which Cooke exploited. Editors should demand corroboration and be cautious when key facts rest on anonymous sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not present composites or fictionalized composites as factual reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid passing off composites or synthesized narratives as literal fact; label or contextualize syntheses appropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooke admitted she "made up the story of Jimmy based on a composite" of accounts; presenting such a composite as a factual profile misleads readers and is abusive of journalistic trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess potential real-world harms and verify before publishing serious allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Before publishing allegations that could trigger official action or harm individuals, ensure rigorous verification because reporting can mobilize authorities and affect custody, safety, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Cooke story led to police searches, social-service mobilization, and a mother temporarily losing custody. The piece uses these consequences to argue for extra care on high-impact stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain transparency and correct the record promptly when errors are discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: When fabrication or error is found, the outlet should acknowledge, apologize, and take corrective steps to regain credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ben Bradlee’s quoted response—apologize to readers and rebuild credibility—plus the Pulitzer being withdrawn, are cited as appropriate remedial actions after the scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let desire for a compelling story override skepticism and verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist editorial temptation to publish a great narrative without adequate verification simply because the story is attractive or controversial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article stresses that editors wanted the Cooke story so badly they ignored warning signs; this bias toward publishable narratives must be checked to prevent fraud.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readers should approach news with a critical eye and verify for themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: “It’s up to readers to read the news with a critical eye, and satisfy themselves that it’s the real deal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece advises consumers to be skeptical, look for verifiable details, and not blindly trust news on any platform. This is guidance for audiences as well as a de facto standard for judging news reliability.
